coverage: U.S.: initial Liberty ship completions and subsequent expansion
chunk_text: Of the ambitious Liberty ship program only seven ships were completed during 1941 and five of those were for the British. But the necessary groundwork had been laid for vast increases in shipbuilding which was to reach its peak in a year and a half.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of the Budget: The United States at War, Chapter VI
rationale: The passage focuses on initial Liberty ship completions and subsequent expansion.

coverage: U.S.: differences in Liberty shipyard productivity
chunk_text: Analyses of comparative performance by individual yards awarded contracts showed marked variations in efficiency. The best yards building Liberty vessels showed a production record for all deliveries during their operating history, of from two to three times that of the poorest yards.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of the Budget: The United States at War, Chapter VI
rationale: The passage focuses on differences in Liberty shipyard productivity.

chunk_text: In his address to Congress of January 6, 1942, the President said that he had ordered immediate steps to be taken "to increase our production rate of merchant ships so rapidly that in this year, 1942, we shall build 8,000,000 deadweight tons as compared with a 1941 production of 1,100,000. We shall continue that increase so that next year, 1943, we shall build 10,000,000 tons."
source_title: U.S. Bureau of the Budget: The United States at War, Chapter VI
rationale: The passage focuses on quantified merchant-shipbuilding targets.

chunk_text: Aircraft production in 1944 not only surpassed the record of any previous year, but also ran closer to schedule than ever before. The industry overcame difficulties that had retarded the aircraft program since 1940.
source_title: War Production Board: War Production in 1944
rationale: The passage focuses on record aircraft production in 1944.

coverage: U.S.: aircraft engine output and its growth
chunk_text: The production of aircraft engines continued to increase, with a 1944 total of more than 259,000, an increase of almost 15 percent over 1943, and an increase of almost 400 percent over 1941. The emphasis shifted in the direction of larger horsepower and new models; the first deliveries of jet engines were included in the 1944 total.
source_title: War Production Board: War Production in 1944
rationale: The passage focuses on aircraft engine output and its growth.

coverage: Germany: aircraft numbers versus airframe-weight growth
chunk_text: German industry's vaunted production of 36,000 aircraft in 1944 was only 8,000 above what the Japanese produced that year. The numerical increase in 1944 over 1943, consisting almost entirely of fighters (a percentage rise of 55.9 percent), hides the fact that German production rose only 23.9 percent in terms of airframe weight.
source_title: U.S. Air Force: Strategy for Defeat, Chapter 6
rationale: The passage focuses on aircraft numbers versus airframe-weight growth.

coverage: Germany: bombing limits output and planned expansion
chunk_text: Unhindered by Allied bombing, German production would have risen far higher and far faster. The target of 80,000-plus aircraft in production plans for 1945 gives an indication of the direction in which Milch and his planners were pushing.
source_title: U.S. Air Force: Strategy for Defeat, Chapter 6
rationale: The passage focuses on bombing limits output and planned expansion.

coverage: Britain: fighter deliveries rise during the Battle of Britain
chunk_text: The delivery of new fighters rose from 256 in April to 467 in September—more than enough to cover the losses—and Fighter Command emerged from the Battle in the autumn with more aircraft than it had possessed at the beginning. The most spectacular, as well as the most important single incident in the history of war production was thus crowned with success.
rationale: The passage focuses on fighter deliveries rise during the Battle of Britain.

coverage: Britain: 29,000 aircraft between Dunkirk and Pearl Harbor
chunk_text: Still more spectacular, even though disappointing to the Air Staff and at times to the Prime Minister, was the output of aircraft. Measured in units of complete aircraft, the total produced between Dunkirk and Pearl Harbor reached 29,000: monthly deliveries of new aircraft are shown in Appendix 4.
rationale: The passage focuses on 29,000 aircraft between Dunkirk and Pearl Harbor.

coverage: Britain: quantified bomber-production requirements and projected shortfall
chunk_text: In order to achieve a first-line strength of 4,000 medium and heavy bombers, the R.A.F. required 22,000 to be made between July 1941 and July 1943; of these 5,500 might be expected from American production. The latest forecast showed that of the remaining 16,500 only 11,000 would be obtained from British factories.
rationale: The passage focuses on quantified bomber-production requirements and projected shortfall.

chunk_text: In 1941, 5,088 planes (more than four times the 1936 output) were made available to the military forces. But the real expansion, the "all-out" national effort, came during the war years, 1942 to 1944. Nearly six times as many airplanes rolled off the lines in 1944 as in 1941.
rationale: The passage focuses on rapid aircraft production expansion, 1941–1944.

coverage: Japan: aircraft and engine output losses from attack and dispersal
chunk_text: Under air attack and dispersion, however, aircraft engine production fell to 1,257 by July 1945 and aircraft production decreased to 1,131. The estimated loss in the production of engines from December 1944 to July 1945 due to direct and indirect effects of air attacks amounted to 11,000 engines, or 43 percent of the number which might have been produced if dispersal and direct attacks had not taken place.

coverage: Exclusion: deployment of Marine aircraft at Midway
chunk_text: The plan for employment of the Marine air group was as follows: The field was to be cleared of all aircraft as soon as radar reported the approach of enemy planes. The fighting squadron was to be directed by radio to intercept the enemy bombers before they reached Midway.
source_title: U.S. Office of Naval Intelligence: The Battle of Midway, Chapter 5
rationale: Exclusion: deployment of Marine aircraft at Midway.

coverage: Exclusion: locating and attacking enemy carriers
chunk_text: A PBY reported two carriers and the main body of ships, carriers in front, course 135°, speed 25, on bearing from Midway 320°, distance 180 miles. Shortly afterwards the B-17's, already on their way to attack the enemy forces to the west, were ordered to change their course and make the carriers their targets.
source_title: U.S. Office of Naval Intelligence: The Battle of Midway, Chapter 5
rationale: Exclusion: locating and attacking enemy carriers.

chunk_text: Of the 27 fighter planes of the Marine air group which intercepted the enemy bombers, 15 were missing and 7 severely damaged. They had, however, inflicted greater damage on the enemy.
